questions.question: Chronic amoebic ulcers of the colon are classically described by which shape, due to undermining of the ulcer margins by the trophozoite's lytic action?
questions.explanation: Chronic amoebic ulcers are described as 'flask-shaped' because the lytic action of Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites undermines and enlarges the ulcer margins beneath a narrower surface opening, giving it a flask-like profile on cross-section.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Amoebiasis

questions.question: Plasmodium falciparum causes markedly more severe (malignant) malaria than the other three plasmodial species mainly because:

options.A: It has an exo-erythrocytic stage that the others lack
options.B: It only infects the liver, never red blood cells
options.C: It parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell multiple times, and makes parasitised red cells sticky, causing capillary obstruction in deep organs
options.D: It is transmitted by a different mosquito genus entirely

questions.explanation: Unlike the other plasmodial species (which parasitise only juvenile red cells and lack these features), P. falciparum parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell with more than one parasite, and makes infected red cells sticky — causing capillary obstruction (e.g. in the brain, producing cerebral malaria) that accounts for its exceptional virulence. It also notably lacks an exo-erythrocytic stage, but that is not the source of its severity.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Malaria

questions.question: Massive haemoglobin absorption by the renal tubules in severe falciparum malaria produces which complication?
questions.explanation: In falciparum malaria, massive absorption of haemoglobin (released by destroyed red cells) by the renal tubules produces blackwater fever, also called haemoglobinuric nephrosis.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Malaria

questions.question: The chronic form of filariasis, characterised by lymphoedema and gross thickening of the skin of the legs/scrotum, is known as:
questions.explanation: Chronic filariasis (caused by Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi) produces lymphadenopathy, lymphoedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis — enormous thickening and induration of the skin, resembling the hide of an elephant, due to chronic lymphatic obstruction.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Filariasis

questions.question: Cysticercosis in humans is most commonly acquired by:

options.B: Eating undercooked pork ('measly pork') or ingesting contaminated vegetables/food carrying Taenia solium eggs

questions.explanation: Cysticercosis is infection by the larval stage of Taenia solium (the pork tapeworm). Humans acquire it by eating undercooked ('measly') pork containing larval cysts, by ingesting food/vegetables contaminated with eggs, or occasionally by autoinfection.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Cysticercosis

questions.question: The acronym TORCH, used for a group of congenital infections with overlapping symptoms, stands for Toxoplasma, Others, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, and:
questions.explanation: TORCH stands for Toxoplasma, Others (hepatitis B, coxsackievirus B, mumps, poliovirus), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex virus — a group of infections tested together in suspected congenital infection because their symptoms in the newborn are often indistinguishable from one another.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — TORCH Complex

questions.question: Among the TORCH agents, which one is most harmful to the fetus specifically when acquired during the first 10 weeks of pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Rubella (German measles) is teratogenic, and infection during the acute stage of the first 10 weeks of pregnancy is far more harmful to the fetus than infection later in gestation, producing the classic congenital rubella syndrome (ocular defects, cardiac defects, CNS manifestations, sensorineural deafness).
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — TORCH Complex

questions.question: Malignant tumours arising from epithelial tissue are generally named:
questions.explanation: Malignant tumours of epithelial origin are called carcinomas, while malignant tumours of mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin are called sarcomas.
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Nomenclature and Classification

questions.question: Which of the following tumour names is a notable EXCEPTION to standard nomenclature, since despite ending in '-oma' (usually implying benign), it actually refers to a malignant tumour?
questions.explanation: Although the suffix '-oma' generally denotes a benign tumour, several names break this rule: melanoma (malignant tumour of melanocytes), hepatoma (a term sometimes used for hepatocellular carcinoma), lymphoma (malignant tumour of lymphoid tissue), and seminoma (malignant testicular tumour) are all malignant despite the '-oma' ending.
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Nomenclature and Classification

questions.question: A hamartoma is best defined as:

options.A: A malignant tumour of embryonal blastema seen mainly in infants
options.B: A benign tumour composed of mature but disorganised cells/tissues that are normally indigenous to that organ
options.C: An ectopic island of otherwise completely normal tissue in the wrong location
options.D: A tumour combining epithelial and mesenchymal malignant elements

questions.explanation: A hamartoma is a benign lesion made up of mature, differentiated tissue elements that are normal to the organ in question, just disorganised/jumbled — e.g. a pulmonary hamartoma contains mature cartilage, smooth muscle, and epithelium, all normal bronchial components arranged abnormally. This is distinct from a choristoma (ectopic normal tissue in the wrong site) and from blastomas (embryonal tumours of children).
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Special Categories of Tumours

questions.question: A choristoma differs from a true neoplasm in that it is actually:

options.A: An ectopic island of otherwise normal tissue (heterotopia), not a genuine tumour
options.B: A tumour with two distinct malignant cell lines mixed together
options.C: Exactly the same thing as a hamartoma
options.D: Always fatal within the first year of life

questions.explanation: A choristoma is the name given to ectopic islands of completely normal tissue found in an abnormal location — it is heterotopia, not a true tumour, even though the name sounds like one.
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Special Categories of Tumours

questions.question: Blastomas (embryomas) such as neuroblastoma, nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour), and retinoblastoma are notable because they:

options.A: Occur almost exclusively in adults over 60
options.B: Arise from embryonal/partially differentiated cells and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5
options.C: Are always benign despite the '-oma' name

questions.explanation: Blastomas arise from embryonal or partially differentiated cells that would normally form the blastema of organs/tissues during embryogenesis, and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5 years of age.
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Special Categories of Tumours

questions.question: The two basic components present in every tumour (benign or malignant) are the parenchyma and the:
questions.explanation: Every tumour has parenchyma (the proliferating tumour cells themselves, which determine the tumour's nature and behaviour) and a supportive stroma (fibrous connective tissue and blood vessels that provide the structural framework for the parenchymal cells to grow on).
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Nomenclature and Classification

questions.question: Carcinosarcoma is an example of a mixed tumour because it combines:

options.A: Two different carcinomas of the same epithelial origin
options.B: A malignant tumour of epithelium (carcinoma) with a malignant tumour of mesenchymal tissue (sarcoma) in the same lesion
options.C: A benign and a malignant tumour of the same tissue type
options.D: Tissue from all three germ cell layers

questions.explanation: Carcinosarcoma is the rare combination of a malignant epithelial tumour (carcinoma) and a malignant mesenchymal tumour (sarcoma) occurring together in the same lesion, such as in the thyroid.
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Special Categories of Tumours

questions.question: Which type of necrosis is most commonly caused by sudden cessation of blood flow (ischaemia), classically affecting the heart, kidney, and spleen?
questions.explanation: Coagulative necrosis is the most common type of necrosis, most often caused by sudden cessation of blood flow (ischaemic necrosis), typically affecting solid organs like the heart, kidney, and spleen — the classic example being a myocardial or renal infarct.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Coagulative Necrosis

questions.question: The hallmark microscopic feature of coagulative necrosis is:

options.A: Complete liquefaction with no recognisable cell outlines
options.B: Preservation of the basic outline of the cell ('tombstones') even though cytoplasmic and nuclear detail is lost
options.C: Cheese-like, structureless material with surrounding granulomatous inflammation
options.D: Formation of calcium soaps from adipocyte breakdown

questions.explanation: In coagulative necrosis, cells are converted into 'tombstones' — their outline and cell type remain recognisable even though the cytoplasmic and nuclear details are lost; unlike liquefactive necrosis, cell digestion and liquefaction do not occur.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Coagulative Necrosis

questions.question: Liquefactive (colliquative) necrosis, seen classically in cerebral infarcts and abscess cavities, occurs because:

options.A: Calcium soaps form and harden the tissue
options.B: Hydrolytic enzymes play a dominant role in tissue degradation, producing semi-fluid material
options.C: The tissue is replaced entirely by fibrous scar with no enzymatic activity
options.D: Granulomatous inflammation surrounds a cheese-like centre

questions.explanation: Liquefactive necrosis occurs commonly from ischaemic injury or bacterial/fungal infection, where hydrolytic enzymes dominate tissue degradation, converting the affected area into semi-fluid material — classic examples are a brain infarct and an abscess cavity.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Liquefaction Necrosis

questions.question: Caseous necrosis, with its characteristic 'cheese-like' gross appearance, is classically found in the centre of which type of lesion?
questions.explanation: Caseous necrosis is found classically in the centre of tuberculous foci — combining features of both coagulative and liquefactive necrosis — with surrounding granulomatous inflammation (epithelioid cells, Langhans' giant cells, and a peripheral lymphocyte mantle).
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Caseous Necrosis

questions.question: In fat necrosis due to acute pancreatitis, free fatty acids released from ruptured adipocytes combine with calcium to form:
questions.explanation: In fat necrosis, liberated pancreatic lipases cause hydrolysis of adipocytes, releasing free fatty acids which complex with calcium to form calcium soaps — a process called saponification, giving the necrotic foci their firm, chalky-white gross appearance.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Fat Necrosis

questions.question: Unlike necrosis, apoptosis is characteristically NOT accompanied by:

options.C: Cell membrane changes of any kind
options.D: Any regulation by the cell itself

questions.explanation: Apoptosis is a controlled, internally programmed form of cell death ('cell suicide') that, unlike necrosis, occurs without triggering inflammation or collateral tissue damage — this is one of the key distinguishing features between the two forms of cell death.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Apoptosis

questions.question: Which of the following is a NORMAL, physiological example of apoptosis rather than a pathological one?

options.A: Cell death in tumours exposed to chemotherapy
options.B: Regression of the lactating breast after breastfeeding is withdrawn

questions.explanation: Physiologic apoptosis includes organised tissue sculpting during embryonic development, hormone-dependent tissue involution (such as regression of the lactating breast after weaning, or endometrial shedding), and normal replacement proliferation in tissues like intestinal epithelium — distinct from pathological apoptosis, such as chemotherapy-induced tumour cell death.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Apoptosis in Biologic Processes

questions.question: Idiopathic (hereditary) haemochromatosis is characterised by a classic triad of pigmentary liver cirrhosis, skin pigmentation, and:

options.A: Pancreatic damage resulting in diabetes mellitus ('bronze diabetes')

questions.explanation: Hereditary haemochromatosis is characterised by a triad: pigmentary liver cirrhosis, pancreatic damage causing diabetes mellitus, and skin pigmentation — earning it the nickname 'bronze diabetes' based on the latter two features.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Pigments, Haemosiderin

questions.question: Lipofuscin, sometimes called the 'wear and tear pigment', is most characteristically associated with:

options.B: Atrophied cells in ageing (e.g. 'brown atrophy' of the heart)

questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is a golden-brown intralysosomal pigment that accumulates in atrophied cells of old age (hence 'wear and tear pigment'), seen in myocardial fibres (producing 'brown atrophy' of the heart), hepatocytes, and neurons in senile dementia.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Lipofuscin

questions.question: Haemozoin (acid haematin, malarial pigment) is distinguished from haemosiderin by which key laboratory feature?

options.A: Haemozoin stains positive with Perl's Prussian blue reaction, while haemosiderin does not
options.B: Haemozoin does NOT stain with Perl's Prussian blue reaction, unlike haemosiderin which does
options.C: Both stain identically with every histochemical stain
options.D: Haemozoin is only found in bone marrow, never other tissue

questions.explanation: Unlike haemosiderin, haemozoin (malarial pigment) does NOT stain with Perl's Prussian blue reaction — likely because it forms a complex with protein that prevents the reaction — despite both being haem-iron-derived pigments.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Acid Haematin
